cultivar: Shiqian Taicha, with Fuding, Mingshan and Longjing varieties also grown
processing: A flat-style green tea, unoxidised, shaped into slightly flattened bud-like pieces with visible down and dried.
harvest_season: Not specifically recorded; spring is the usual prized picking for a bud-style Guizhou green.
appearance_dry: Natural bud shapes, slightly flattened and downy, in an even, glossy green.
taste_profile: Clean, fresh aroma with a brisk, savoury-fresh flavour.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a flat green. Use water around 80°C; downy buds can turn sharp with hotter water and long steeps.

vintage_note: Normally bought as the current spring tea and best within the year, as is usual for Chinese greens. The geographical indication covers 18 townships and the main plant is a local one, so a packet naming both place and variety tells you more.
description:
Shiqian Taicha comes from Shiqian county in northeast Guizhou, on the slope down from the Yunnan-Guizhou plateau to the hills of western Hunan. It is built around a local tea plant of the same name, and it is one of the teas regularly named among Guizhou's best known.

It is made as a flat-style green: slightly pressed, downy bud shapes with a glossy green colour. Local plantings also include Fuding, Mingshan and Longjing varieties, and osmanthus and other trees are sometimes planted between the rows.

The cup is bright yellow-green with a clean aroma and a fresh, brisk flavour. Brew it as you would a Long Jing-style tea, with water around 80°C and no long steeps early on.

When buying, check for whole, even buds and a clear harvest date. The name is well protected, as a geographical indication and certification mark, but the label does not always say which plant variety was used, so it is worth asking.
history:
The Wanli-era Guizhou provincial gazetteer is cited locally for the statement that Shiqian tea began under the Tang and that growing and drinking flourished by the early Ming. It is the main early reference, and it reaches modern readers through later local accounts.

The modern industry took off around the turn of this century. The tea took gold at the 1999 international tea expo and a top prize at that year's Zhongcha Cup, and in February 2008 it became a national agricultural standardisation project. It was recognised as a geographical certification mark in 2010, as a well-known trademark in 2013, and as a national agricultural geographical indication on 10 February 2015.
